table.text: Participants from the general public were recruited via flyers distributed in public spaces across the Wellington region (e.g., libraries, bus stops, supermarkets).
Student participants were recruited from the Introduction to Psychological Research Programmes (IPRP) at the two universities.
Prolific participants received financial compensation, community participants were entered into a prize draw, and students received credit toward their course.

Ethnic composition broadly reflected that of the general population (78% European, 16% Māori, 15% Asian, 5% Pacific, 4% MELAA, compared with 68%, 18%, 17%, 9%, and 2% respectively; Stats NZ, 2023), although European participants were over-represented and Pacific participants under-represented.
Most participants were students (79%), and 39% held a university degree.
Participants were asked to rate their support for each power on a 5-point scale from 'strongly oppose' to 'strongly support' (α = .90).
Participants were asked: "Does the NZ Police having extra powers to deal with gangs make you feel more safe, less safe or does it make no difference?"

We also accounted for whether participants had recent contact with police in the previous two years (1 = police contact,0 = no contact), and whether they had exposure to gangs in the past 12 months (how often they had seen someone in public wearing a gang patch; 5-point scale, ranging from never to very often).

Participants were most supportive of dispersal notices preventing gathering in public spaces (56%), followed by search powers for repeat insignia breaches (46%), and least supportive of arresting individuals for wearing gang insignia (36%).

Compared with the 2023 Census, European participants were over-represented and Pacific peoples were under-represented, and our recruitment strategy did not specifically target the communities most likely to be directly affected by the new powers.
Written informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Prolific Academic is an online crowdsourcing platform that connects researchers with participants (Peer et al., 2022).
Participants from the general public were recruited via flyers distributed in public spaces across the Wellington region (e.g., libraries, bus stops, supermarkets).
Student participants were recruited from the Introduction to Psychological Research Programmes (IPRP) at the two universities.
Prolific participants received financial compensation, community participants were entered into a prize draw, and students received credit toward their course.

Ethnic composition broadly reflected that of the general population (78% European, 16% Māori, 15% Asian, 5% Pacific, 4% MELAA, compared with 68%, 18%, 17%, 9%, and 2% respectively; Stats NZ, 2023), although European participants were over-represented and Pacific participants under-represented.
Most participants were students (79%), and 39% held a university degree.
Participants were asked to rate their support for each power on a 5-point scale from 'strongly oppose' to 'strongly support' (α = .90).
Participants were asked: "Does the NZ Police having extra powers to deal with gangs make you feel more safe, less safe or does it make no difference?"

We also accounted for whether participants had recent contact with police in the previous two years (1 = police contact,0 = no contact), and whether they had exposure to gangs in the past 12 months (how often they had seen someone in public wearing a gang patch; 5-point scale, ranging from never to very often).

Participants were most supportive of dispersal notices preventing gathering in public spaces (56%), followed by search powers for repeat insignia breaches (46%), and least supportive of arresting individuals for wearing gang insignia (36%).

Compared with the 2023 Census, European participants were over-represented and Pacific peoples were under-represented, and our recruitment strategy did not specifically target the communities most likely to be directly affected by the new powers.
Written informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants.

text.text: In many jurisdictions, police are periodically granted new powers intended to reduce crime and enhance community safety, raising questions about the conditions under which the public supports expanded police authority.

The Gangs Act 2024 granted the New Zealand Police new powers to restrict gang activity, including the authority to arrest individuals for displaying gang insignia in public and to disperse gang gatherings in public spaces.

Drawing on survey data from a non-representative sample of 766 adult residents of Aotearoa New Zealand, we examine normative (procedural justice and legitimacy), instrumental (police effectiveness and fear of crime), and affective predictors of public support for these powers.
Affective responses (feeling safer at the prospect of the new powers) were the strongest predictor of support, and accounted for much of the association between the other predictors and support.
Procedural justice was associated with support directly and indirectly, mainly via affective responses.
Right-wing political orientation and fear of crime were associated with higher support, and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals predicted lower support.
Police effectiveness was positively correlated with support but negatively associated with it once fairness was accounted for.
This study extends the police empowerment literature to the context of powers targeted at a specific, socially stigmatised group.

Our findings suggest that support for such powers is more closely tied to how they make people feel than to judgements about police effectiveness, and that those with personal contact with gangaffiliated individuals are less supportive, raising questions about public opinion as a basis for justifying targeted police powers.
In many jurisdictions, police rely on the voluntary cooperation and compliance of the public to effectively uphold and enforce the law.
Securing public support becomes especially important when police adopt new powers or technologies that have the potential to significantly affect the communities they serve.

Powers introduced without sufficient public backing risk provoking backlash, undermining police legitimacy, and proving difficult to enforce in practice, given that compliance rests largely on consent rather than coercion (Sunshine & Tyler, 2003; Tyler & Fagan, 2008).

text.text: Questions of public support have been central to debates over the expansion of police powers during the COVID-19 pandemic (Yesberg et al., 2024), police militarisation (Moule et al., 2019), and the adoption of live facial recognition technology (Bradford et al., 2020).

text.text: The introduction of the Gangs Act 2024 presents a recent such case in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ).
Under the Act, displaying gang insignia in public places became an offence, and police were given powers to enforce this ban and to disperse gang gatherings in public spaces (Gangs Act 2024).
As with new powers introduced in other contexts, the long-term effectiveness of these powers depends, in part, on the level of public support they receive.

Research on public support for police empowerment has commonly distinguished between normative motivations-grounded in trust that police authority is legitimate and will be used responsibly-and instrumental motivations, grounded in outcome-based judgements about whether new powers will be effective in reducing crime and improving public safety (Bradford et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2021; Sargeant et al., 2024).

text.text: Both involve relatively deliberate evaluations, of either the police or the likely outcomes of their powers.
However, support may also depend on people's more immediate affective responses to new powers, which do not map neatly onto either motivation.
Unlike trust or outcome-based judgements, affective reactions may function as a heuristic: a quicker, less deliberative response to a policy (Slovic et al., 2002 (Slovic et al., , 2004)).

text.text: This study draws on the police empowerment literature to examine support for the Gangs Act 2024 in NZ.
However, the Gangs Act differs from most prior instances of police empowerment studied in the literature in two important ways.
First, unlike powers directed at the general public, those granted under the Gangs Act target a specific and socially stigmatised subset of the population: gang-affiliated individuals.

Second, unlike prior instances of police empowerment, which have often been initiated by police services (e.g., live facial recognition), the powers granted under the Gangs Act originated as government legislation that was introduced as part of a coalition commitment to "restoring law and order" (NZ Government, 2024).

text.text: As a result, public support for the Act may reflect not only perceptions of police, but also broader punitive orientations toward gang-affiliated individuals.

We therefore examine the normative, instrumental, and affective predictors of support identified in the police empowerment literature alongside factors known to shape punitive attitudes, such as political orientation and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals (Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010; Rade et al., 2016).

text.text: Gangs have long been a part of the social landscape of NZ, often emerging within communities affected by colonisation, poverty, and alienation.

Modern gangs began to form in the 1950s and 1960s, comprising predominantly young Pākehā (European) men drawn to a nomadic lifestyle centred on motorcycling and the rejection of mainstream cultural norms.

This period also saw the rise of the Hells Angels, the first clearly patched and organised outlaw motorcycle gang in NZ, and with it a shift toward more organised and violent activity (Gilbert, 2013).

text.text: During this period, gangs began recruiting disenfranchised young Māori seeking belonging and identity, and a means of resisting the structures that had excluded them (Gilbert, 2013; Taonui & Newbold, 2012; Webb, 2017).

text.text: As gangs expanded their presence across NZ, their relationship with the police became increasingly strained.

From the 1970s onwards, both the Government and Police shifted toward more overt suppression strategies, with parliament introducing numerous legislative amendments aimed at criminalising gang membership, restricting association, and expanding police powers to intervene in gang spaces (Gilbert, 2013).

text.text: Yet, little is known about how the wider NZ public views the Act.

Policing in NZ operates on the principle of policing by consent (NZ Police, 2020); hence, understanding public support for the Act is important because it may partly determine the Act's implementation, effectiveness, and broader social impact.

Affect has typically been operationalised through items capturing people's emotional and behavioural responses to a particular power; for example, whether the presence of an armed officer makes a person feel safer and more comfortable approaching them (Yesberg & Bradford, 2019).

text.text: Affect and trust are closely linked: affective responses to an unfamiliar policy or technology are shaped, in part, by the extent to which people trust the actors responsible for implementing it (Midden & Huijts, 2009).

text.text: In both studies, affect mediated the relationship between procedural justice, effectiveness, and support for the new powers.

The factors reviewed above help explain why people support expanding police authority in general, but the Gangs Act 2024 differs from most police empowerment cases in targeting a specific, socially stigmatised group.
Public support for the Act may therefore also reflect punitive attitudes toward gang-affiliated individuals, independent of views about police authority.
We next consider two factors relevant to these attitudes: political orientation and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals.

Political orientation, typically measured on a left-right or liberal-conservative scale, is one of the most consistent predictors of punitive attitudes toward offenders (Rade et al., 2016). Jost et al. (2003) argue that political conservatism is, in part, a form of motivated social cognition: a response to a psychological need to manage uncertainty and threat, reflected in traits such as intolerance of ambiguity, resistance to change, and heightened sensitivity to perceived danger.

(2003)</ref> argue that political conservatism is, in part, a form of motivated social cognition: a response to a psychological need to manage uncertainty and threat, reflected in traits such as intolerance of ambiguity, resistance to change, and heightened sensitivity to perceived danger.

text.text: This threat-management account offers a plausible mechanism for why political conservatism is linked to more punitive attitudes toward groups seen as socially disruptive or threatening, such as gang-affiliated individuals.

More broadly, scholars have noted that punitive policies directed at socially marginalised groups frequently feature in populist 'law and order' political strategies that emphasise social threat and disorder (Pratt & Clark, 2005; Wacquant, 2009).

text.text: Such strategies may resonate with individuals who prioritise safety and social stability, particularly when the targeted group is already stigmatised.
The Gangs Act may therefore represent a context in which broader ideological orientations are closely tied to willingness to expand police authority.

A meta-analysis by Rade et al. (2016) found that individuals with more conservative political orientations held more negative attitudes toward people with criminal convictions, while Hirschfield and Piquero (2010) found that conservative ideology was associated with more negative evaluations of formerly incarcerated individuals.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that a right-wing political orientation may be associated with greater support for expanding police powers, particularly when directed toward groups perceived as threatening the existing social order, such as gang-affiliated individuals.

Intergroup Contact Theory (ICT), first proposed by Allport (1954), suggests that the frequency, quality, and context of contact between members of different social groups shape the attitudes they hold toward one another.
text.formatted: Intergroup Contact Theory (ICT), first proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Allport (1954)</ref>, suggests that the frequency, quality, and context of contact between members of different social groups shape the attitudes they hold toward one another.

text.text: According to the theory, positive social contact reduces prejudice and fosters more favourable perceptions across group boundaries.

Research has identified the mechanisms through which contact reduces prejudice, including reduced intergroup anxiety, increased empathy and perspective taking, and greater knowledge of the outgroup (Pettigrew et al., 2011).

text.text: Studies consistently show that individuals who know someone with a criminal conviction, or who have had meaningful interactions with formerly incarcerated people, tend to hold less stigmatising and more supportive attitudes toward this population (Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010; Rade et al., 2016).

text.text: Conversely, those with little or no previous contact often express more negative, stereotyped, or punitive views.

Taken together, these findings suggest that contact with gang-affiliated individuals may foster more favourable attitudes and reduce support for new police powers that could negatively impact on them.

The literature reviewed above identifies a well-established set of predictors of support for police empowerment, but this research focuses on powers affecting the general public (e.g., militarisation, surveillance, pandemic enforcement) and is largely concentrated in the US and UK.
It is unclear whether these predictors will operate in the same way when powers target a specific, stigmatised group, and no research on police empowerment has been conducted in NZ.
The Gangs Act 2024 provides a novel opportunity to address these gaps.

We draw on the police empowerment literature-normative motivations (procedural justice, legitimacy), instrumental motivations (police effectiveness, fear of crime), and affective responses-alongside the literature on punitive attitudes (political orientation and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals) to examine predictors of support for the new policing powers (see Figure 1).

text.text: We test the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 1: Perceptions of police legitimacy and affective responses will be positively associated with support for the Gangs Act.

Hypothesis 2: Perceptions of procedural justice, police effectiveness, fear of crime, and right-wing political orientation will be positively associated with support for the Gangs Act, while interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals will be negatively associated with support for the Gangs Act.

Hypothesis 3: Perceptions of procedural justice, police effectiveness, fear of crime, right-wing political orientation, and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals will be indirectly associated with support for the Gangs Act via police legitimacy and affect.

Police empowerment was operationalised as participants' support for expanded police powers to restrict gangs.

We assessed support for three new powers introduced under the Gangs Act 2024: the police's ability to (1) arrest individuals for wearing gang patches in public; (2) search the homes of individuals who repeatedly breach the ban on gang insignia; and (3) issue dispersal notices to stop gang members from gathering in public spaces.
Participants were asked to rate their support for each power on a 5-point scale from 'strongly oppose' to 'strongly support' (α = .90).

Affective responses were measured with one item asking participants whether the new gang-related powers made them feel more or less safe, consistent with how prior studies have operationalised affect (Yesberg et al., 2024; Yesberg & Bradford, 2019).

text.text: Participants were asked: "Does the NZ Police having extra powers to deal with gangs make you feel more safe, less safe or does it make no difference?"

Police legitimacy was measured as two related but distinct constructs (Jackson et al., 2023).

text.text: Normative alignment captured the extent to which participants perceived police values and behaviour as consistent with their own, using three items: (1) "I support the way the police usually act", (2) "the police usually act in ways that are consistent with my own ideas about what is right and wrong", and (3) "the police stand up for values that are important for people like me" (α = .90).

Obligation to obey captured the perceived moral duty to comply with police directives, also measured with three items : "To what extent do you agree or disagree it is your moral duty to… (1) obey the police; (2) support the decisions of police officers, even if you disagree with them; (3) do what the police tell you even if you don't understand or agree with the reasons" (α = .82).
Participants responded to both sets of items on a 5-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'.

Procedural justice was measured using four items assessing perceptions of police fairness and quality of interpersonal treatment, including whether police (1) treat people fairly, (2) treat people with dignity and respect, (3) listen before making decisions, and (4) explain their decisions (Sunshine & Tyler, 2003).

text.text: Participants responded on a 5-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' (α = .87).

Perceived police effectiveness was assessed using three items capturing participants' evaluations of whether the NZ Police are effective at (1) solving crime, (2) preventing crime, and (3) maintaining order.
Participants responded on a 5-point scale ranging from 'not at all effective' to 'very effective' (α = .79).
Fear of crime was measured with three items assessing participants' level of worry about crime, antisocial behaviour, and gang activity in their local area.
Participants responded on a 5-point scale from 'not at all worried' to 'very worried' (α = .82).
Interpersonal contact was measured by asking participants whether they personally knew someone who is, or had been, involved in a gang (1 = contact,0 = no contact).
Political orientation was measured using a single item on a 7-point scale, ranging from very left-wing to very right-wing (Bradford et al., 2020).

text.text: Additional demographic and experiential variables were included as controls to account for confounding factors that could also be associated with support for police powers.

Demographic variables included age (continuous variable), gender identity (1 = male,0 = female or non-binary), ethnicity (five non-exclusive binary variables: European, Māori, Pacific Peoples, Asian, and MELAA), country of birth (1 = NZ,0 = not-NZ), education (1 = university degree,0 = no degree), and employment status (three non-exclusive binary variables: 'employed', 'student', 'unemployed').

We also accounted for whether participants had recent contact with police in the previous two years (1 = police contact,0 = no contact), and whether they had exposure to gangs in the past 12 months (how often they had seen someone in public wearing a gang patch; 5-point scale, ranging from never to very often).

Three items were added to the survey after data collection had begun, so they were not presented to an initial group of participants: worry about gang activity (n = 38 missing), exposure to gangs (n = 39), and interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals (n = 73).
For the worry item, we imputed the mean of participants' responses to the other two fear of crime items.
We first used Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) in the R package lavaan to assess the scaling properties and empirical distinctiveness of the latent constructs.
All observed indicators were set to ordinal, except the fear of crime item with imputed values, which was treated as continuous.
The model was estimated using diagonally weighted least squares estimation with robust standard errors.
Scaled fit statistics indicated the measurement model was a good fit for the data (N = 766; CFI = 0.979; TLI = 0.974; RMSEA = 0.046).
Factor scores from the CFA were saved and used to compute the bivariate correlations reported in Table 2.

Among the control variables, men (β = .075, p = .011) and older participants (β = .091, p = .043) were more supportive of the new powers.
No ethnic group differed significantly from others in direct support once other variables were accounted for.
However, ethnicity was associated with the mediating variables.

Māori participants reported lower normative alignment (β = -.102, p = .020) and felt less safe at the prospect of the new powers (affect β = -.099, p = .019), as did MELAA participants (affect β = -.098, p = .019), with a similar but non-significant pattern for Pacific participants (affect β = -.074, p = .056).
In contrast, Asian participants felt safer (affect β = .142, p = .012) and reported a stronger obligation to obey (β = .123, p = .047).

This study examined public support for the new police powers introduced under the Gangs Act 2024 in Aotearoa New Zealand.
In doing so, it extends the police empowerment literature to powers directed at a specific and highly stigmatised group, rather than the general population.
Support for the Gangs Act varied across the three powers examined.

The highest proportion of participants supported dispersal notices preventing gang members from gathering in public and the lowest proportion supported arrest powers for the display of gang insignia, suggesting the public may be more willing to endorse powers perceived as addressing immediate public safety concerns and less willing to support powers that criminalise identity or expression.

Affective responses emerged as the strongest overall predictor of support, and accounted for much of the association between procedural justice, political orientation, fear of crime, and interpersonal contact and support for the Gangs Act.
Participants who felt safer at the prospect of new powers were significantly more likely to support them.
Although our measure of affect could overlap with support itself, supplementary analyses indicated the two constructs were empirically distinct (see Supplementary Appendix).

This finding is consistent with the affect heuristic, which suggests that individuals often rely on emotional responses rather than systematic evaluation when forming judgements about complex or unfamiliar issues (Slovic et al., 2002 (Slovic et al., , 2004)).

text.text: In the present context, the prospect of new gang-related powers may evoke particularly strong emotional reactions because gangs are highly stigmatised and frequently portrayed in public and political discourse as being associated with danger, disorder, and harm (Bull, 2017; Lewis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In the present context, the prospect of new gang-related powers may evoke particularly strong emotional reactions because gangs are highly stigmatised and frequently portrayed in public and political discourse as being associated with danger, disorder, and harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bull, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lewis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, participants may have relied substantially on how safe the powers made them feel, rather than on a detailed evaluation of the policies.

This pattern is consistent with prior police empowerment research in which affective responses to police powers have emerged as a key predictor of support (Yesberg et al., 2024; Yesberg & Bradford, 2019).

text.text: Procedural justice also emerged as a consistent predictor of support for the new powers.
Participants who viewed the police as fair and respectful were significantly more likely to endorse the powers introduced by the Gangs Act.
Procedural justice was associated with support both directly and indirectly, through obligation to obey police, and, more strongly, through affect.

These findings align with procedural justice theory and prior research on police empowerment, which shows that perceptions of police fairness are associated with greater support for police powers, partly by enhancing police legitimacy (Sargeant et al., 2024; Sunshine & Tyler, 2003; Yesberg et al., 2024).

text.text: In the present study, the indirect association between procedural justice and support for police empowerment via obligation to obey was modest, and procedural justice was associated with support mainly through how safe people felt about the new powers.

Obligation to obey was significantly associated with support, while normative alignment was not; however, the two coefficients were identical in size and did not differ significantly from one another.

Although the constructs were empirically distinct, the model may not have been able to separate the unique contributions of procedural justice and normative alignment because they were strongly correlated.
Hence, both obligation to obey and normative alignment may be relevant for understanding support for the new powers.
By contrast, instrumental motivations played a more limited role in explaining support for police empowerment.
Police effectiveness was positively correlated with support for police empowerment at the bivariate level.

However, the SEM revealed a suppression effect, with the direct path between police effectiveness and support turning negative once other factors, particularly perceptions of fairness, were accounted for.
In other words, believing the police are effective did not contribute positively to support for these powers beyond perceptions of fairness.

One plausible explanation lies in the Gangs Act's focus on suppressing the visibility of gangs, rather than preventing crime, which may make judgements about police effectiveness less relevant to support than for powers framed more directly around outcomes.

In the context of COVID-19 enforcement, for example, perceived police effectiveness remained positively associated with support for police empowerment after accounting for procedural justice, and concerns about health risk were the strongest predictor (Sargeant et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In the context of COVID-19 enforcement, for example, perceived police effectiveness remained positively associated with support for police empowerment after accounting for procedural justice, and concerns about health risk were the strongest predictor <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sargeant et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, fear of crime was only a weak direct predictor of support for the Gangs Act.

These findings are consistent with prior research showing that perceptions of fairness outweigh instrumental concerns in predicting support for police empowerment (Bradford et al., 2020; Kuen et al., 2025; Miethe et al., 2019), and underscore the importance of perceived fairness relative to judgements about police effectiveness.

text.text: Right-wing political orientation was also associated with support, both directly and via affect.
This finding is consistent with Jost et al.'s (2003) account of conservatism as motivated social cognition in response to uncertainty and threat.
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with <ref type="bibr">Jost et al.'s (2003)</ref> account of conservatism as motivated social cognition in response to uncertainty and threat.

text.text: Gangs, frequently framed as disruptive and threatening, are the kind of group toward which this account would predict greater support for coercive responses among those on the political right.

This interpretation aligns with prior research linking conservative or right-wing orientation to more punitive and stigmatising attitudes toward people who offend (Gerber & Jackson, 2016; Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010; Oldfield & Mills, 2022; Rade et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with prior research linking conservative or right-wing orientation to more punitive and stigmatising attitudes toward people who offend <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gerber & Jackson, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Oldfield & Mills, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Rade et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: That this association was partly accounted for by affect suggests that ideological differences may be expressed, in part, through how the new powers make people feel. Oldfield and Mills (2022) found that right-wing participants agreed more often with arguments for less punitive sentences when those arguments used populist rhetoric, suggesting that how criminal justice issues are framed can influence the link between political orientation and punitive attitudes.

text.text: By the same logic, discourse framing gangs as a threat may similarly have strengthened the association between right-wing orientation and feelings of safety under the new powers.
Future research could test this directly, for example by experimentally varying how the powers are framed.

Interpersonal contact with gang-affiliated individuals was associated with lower support for the new powers, both directly and via affect: participants who knew someone involved in a gang felt less safe, not more, at the prospect of police having these powers.
For people with these connections, the powers may be less likely to evoke an abstract threat and more likely to evoke thoughts of the people they know, and how the powers could affect those people.

This interpretation is consistent with Intergroup Contact Theory (Allport, 1954) and with research showing that knowing someone with a criminal conviction is associated with less stigmatising attitudes toward that group (Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010; Rade et al., 2016), as personal contact replaces stereotyped associations with more individualised knowledge (Pettigrew et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with Intergroup Contact Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allport, 1954)</ref> and with research showing that knowing someone with a criminal conviction is associated with less stigmatising attitudes toward that group <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hirschfield & Piquero, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Rade et al., 2016)</ref>, as personal contact replaces stereotyped associations with more individualised knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pettigrew et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, our measure of interpersonal contact was a single binary item asking whether participants knew someone who is, or had been, involved in a gang.
It did not capture the closeness, frequency, or quality of contact, all of which are central to Intergroup Contact Theory, and negative contact may have quite different effects.
In addition, because the data are cross-sectional, alternative explanations for the findings cannot be ruled out.

People who know someone affiliated with a gang may differ from those who do not in ways not fully captured by our controls, such as living in communities more heavily affected by gangs or by over-or under-policing, or having more negative personal or family experiences with police.

The association may also run in the opposite direction: people who already hold less punitive attitudes may be more open to relationships with, or more willing to acknowledge knowing, gang-affiliated individuals.
Future research using longitudinal designs and more detailed measures of contact would help clarify the mechanism.
Nevertheless, regardless of its cause, the association between interpersonal contact and lower support has practical implications.
People who know gang-affiliated individuals, and who may also be more likely to be affected by these powers, were less supportive of them.
If this lower support extends to reduced cooperation with enforcement, it could undermine the powers' implementation and effectiveness.

Analysis of the control variables showed that Māori participants reported lower normative alignment (i.e., the belief that police share their values) and felt less safe than non-Māori participants at the prospect of the new police powers.
Given the central role of affect in explaining support, these findings suggest the powers may be met with greater resistance among Māori communities, in which they are most likely to be applied.
This pattern needs to Pacific participants also showed lower feelings of safety, although this difference was not statistically significant, which may reflect limited statistical power.
Because subgroup sizes in this non-representative sample were relatively small, these findings should be interpreted with caution.
This study has several limitations that should be noted.
First, the use of a nonprobability sample, comprising predominantly young university students, limits the generalisability of the findings to the wider NZ population.

Compared with the 2023 Census, European participants were over-represented and Pacific peoples were under-represented, and our recruitment strategy did not specifically target the communities most likely to be directly affected by the new powers.
That said, a substantial minority of participants (41%) knew someone involved in a gang, so the sample was not entirely removed from those communities.
Second, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference.

Although our findings are consistent with theoretical expectations, the temporal direction of relationships between procedural justice, legitimacy, affect, interpersonal contact, and support for the new powers cannot be established with the current data.

Recent longitudinal research suggests the relationship between procedural justice and police legitimacy may be weaker or more mixed when examined over time (Kuen & Weisburd, 2025; Pina-Sánchez & Brunton-Smith, 2020).

text.text: This limitation reflects broader challenges in the field, where few experimental or longitudinal studies have been conducted to isolate the causal impact of procedural justice on attitudes toward police (Nagin & Telep, 2020).
text.formatted: This limitation reflects broader challenges in the field, where few experimental or longitudinal studies have been conducted to isolate the causal impact of procedural justice on attitudes toward police <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Nagin & Telep, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, some of our measures were not optimal because they relied on simplified or narrow indicators that did not fully capture the underlying psychological constructs they were intended to represent.
Affect was measured using only a single item about feelings of safety, which does not capture the full range of emotions the new powers might elicit (e.g., anger, anxiety, distrust).
Moreover, because the item asked whether the powers made participants feel safer, it may partly capture perceived benefits of the powers rather than affect alone.

Police effectiveness was measured in general terms rather than in relation to the Gangs Act powers themselves, so we cannot assess whether perceptions of the powers' likely effectiveness shaped support.

Lastly, political orientation was measured with a single leftright item, which collapses a multidimensional construct (e.g., economic, social, and authoritarian attitudes) and lacks the nuance of established constructs such as right-wing authoritarianism.
This study examined public support for the Gangs Act 2024 and the factors associated with willingness to grant police new, targeted powers in NZ.
Drawing on a survey of 766 adults, it extends the police empowerment literature to powers aimed at a specific, stigmatised subgroup of the population.

Affective responses-feeling safer at the prospect of the new powers-were the strongest predictor of support, and accounted for much of the association between procedural justice, political orientation, fear of crime, and interpersonal contact and support.

Procedural justice was also a significant direct predictor, and perceptions of police fairness mattered more than perceptions of police effectiveness, consistent with prior research on police empowerment (Bradford et al., 2020; Kuen et al., 2025; Miethe et al., 2019; Sargeant et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Procedural justice was also a significant direct predictor, and perceptions of police fairness mattered more than perceptions of police effectiveness, consistent with prior research on police empowerment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bradford et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kuen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Miethe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Sargeant et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, procedural justice was associated with support more through affect than through police legitimacy.
Right-wing political orientation was also associated with greater support, largely via affect.
The centrality of affective responses raises a concern about the basis on which new powers are justified.

If public support reflects how safe new powers make people feel, rather than a considered evaluation of their costs, benefits, and evidence, then public opinion alone is a limited basis for introducing new, targeted police powers.

This concern is reinforced by our finding on interpersonal contact: participants who knew someone involved in a gang, and who may be more likely to be affected by the powers, were less supportive of them and felt less safe at the prospect of them than those without such contact.
Māori participants, who are among those most likely to be subject to the new powers, also felt less safe at the prospect of the new powers than non-Māori participants.

For police, demonstrating fairness to the general public may help secure broad support for expanded powers, but earning the trust of the communities closest to those powers is likely to be the more meaningful test of whether this authority can be exercised legitimately and effectively.

A similar movement towards symbolically targeting gang identity resurfaced in the 2020s when opposition parties (later forming the coalition Government) largely rejected the findings of an expert report that recommended addressing the social causes of gang formation (Office of the Prime Minister's Chief Science Advisor, 2023), in favour of stronger police enforcement powers modelled on Australian jurisdictions, such as Western Australia's Criminal Law (Unlawful Consorting and Prohibited Insignia) Act, 2021.

The Gangs Act 2024, which came into force on 21 November 2024, expanded police powers to enforce a nationwide prohibition of gang insignia, search for prohibited items, and disperse gang gatherings in public.
Two components of the Act are most relevant to police powers.
First, the Act prohibits the display of gang insignia (excluding tattoos and plain coloured clothing) in public places and specifies penalties for breaching this ban.
